title: Yogurt: protein, calcium, fat and nutritional value

seo.title: Yogurt: protein, calcium, fat and nutritional value
seo.meta_description: Yogurt provides protein and calcium, but numbers vary widely between plain, Greek, whole-milk, nonfat and sweetened products. Here is what a serving really provides.
seo.search_intent: Understand yogurt nutrition and how protein, calcium, fat and sugars differ among common types.

excerpt: Plain yogurt is a useful source of protein and calcium, but there is no single nutrition profile for all yogurt. Conventional plain yogurt often provides roughly 3–5 g protein per 100 g, while Greek yogurt can reach about 8–10 g; fat depends mainly on whether the starting milk is whole, reduced-fat or nonfat.
content_html:
Two cups labeled yogurt can look nearly identical while one contains twice the protein or several times the fat of the other. Yogurt describes a fermentation process, not one fixed nutrient profile.

What plain yogurt provides

Yogurt retains much of milk's protein, calcium and other nutrients while fermentation converts some lactose into lactic acid. Official food-composition references place many conventional plain yogurts around 3–5 g protein per 100 g.

A 125 g serving therefore provides roughly 4–6 g protein. That is useful, but substantially less than a strained Greek-style yogurt.

Why Greek yogurt is usually higher in protein

Traditional Greek yogurt is concentrated by removing part of the whey. With less water, protein becomes more concentrated per 100 g. Many plain Greek yogurts provide about 8–10 g protein per 100 g, roughly double conventional plain yogurt.

That does not automatically make Greek yogurt better. A lighter plain yogurt may suit someone who wants a less dense product. The actual label matters.

Fermentation does not remove the calcium

Yogurt remains a meaningful calcium source. The exact amount varies with the starting milk and manufacturing process; many plain yogurts provide roughly 120–180 mg calcium per 100 g. A 125 g serving can therefore supply around 150–225 mg.

Highly strained products can lose some calcium with the whey, so more protein does not necessarily mean more calcium.

Fat depends mostly on the milk

Nonfat yogurt can be near 0–0.5 g fat per 100 g, while whole-milk plain yogurt commonly sits around 3–4 g/100 g. Some full-fat Greek yogurts are considerably higher.

Fat contributes texture and energy. When comparing products, look at total and saturated fat along with protein and sugars rather than calories alone.

Natural sugar is not the same as added sugar

Plain yogurt naturally contains lactose. Sweetened or flavored yogurt may contain added sugars on top of that lactose. A yogurt with 5 g versus 13 g total sugars per 100 g may therefore represent a very different formulation.

The practical choice

If protein is the priority, compare grams per serving. If calcium matters, check the label because strained products vary. For a simple everyday option, plain unsweetened yogurt is usually the easiest starting point to interpret.

faq.question: How much protein is in yogurt?
faq.answer: Conventional plain yogurt often provides about 3–5 g per 100 g, while many plain Greek yogurts provide roughly 8–10 g/100 g.

faq.question: Is yogurt high in calcium?
faq.answer: It can be a meaningful source. Many plain yogurts provide around 120–180 mg calcium per 100 g, though products vary.

faq.question: Is Greek yogurt always healthier?
faq.answer: No. It is usually higher in protein, but can also be higher in fat and not necessarily higher in calcium. The specific product matters.
